analysis.one_liner: Bans most state-law class actions alleging stock fraud, forcing them into the stricter federal system.
analysis.headline: Congress barred investors from bringing most state-court class actions over stock fraud, and the bill became law in November 1998 after passing the Senate 79-21 and the House 319-82.
analysis.plain_summary: This law stops investors from suing companies for securities fraud as a class under state law, in either state or federal court, when the stock is nationally traded. Defendants can move any such case filed in state court to federal court, where the stricter 1995 federal rules for securities suits apply. States and state pension plans kept the right to sue on their own behalf, state securities regulators kept their enforcement powers, and the bill separately reauthorized funding for the Securities and Exchange Commission for fiscal 1999.
analysis.who_benefits: Publicly traded companies, their officers and directors, and the insurers that cover them gain the most: they can no longer face parallel fraud class actions in state courts, which after the 1995 federal litigation reforms had become the friendlier venue for investors. Companies face fewer suits, lower settlement exposure, and federal cases where early discovery is frozen. The securities plaintiffs' bar loses a major revenue stream.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Publicly traded companies and their insurers

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits any private class action based on state law alleging misstatements, omissions, or deceptive conduct in the purchase or sale of a nationally traded security, in either state or federal court.

Lets defendants remove any covered class action filed in state court to federal district court, where the stricter pleading and procedure rules of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995 apply, including a stay that freezes discovery early in the case.
Closes what Congress called a shift of securities class actions into state courts after the 1995 reform law, which Congress found had prevented that law from achieving its objectives.

Extends the federal discovery stay so plaintiffs cannot keep gathering evidence in state court while a federal case is frozen, preventing parallel state proceedings from working around the federal rules.

Preserves state securities regulators' power to investigate and bring enforcement actions, and preserves the right of states, political subdivisions, and state pension plans to sue on their own behalf or as a class of other government entities.

analysis.who_pays: Investors who bought fraud-tainted shares, including workers whose 401(k)s and private pension funds hold those shares, bear the cost. They lose the state-law route, which had weaker pleading requirements and no automatic freeze on evidence-gathering, and are left with federal claims that are harder to bring and survive. The private securities class-action bar also loses a large part of its docket.

drawbacks.text: Investors defrauded by companies lose their ability to bring state-law fraud class actions, which had allowed cases to proceed with weaker pleading requirements and without the automatic freeze on discovery that federal law imposes; after this law only the harder federal route remains.

The carve-out that preserves the right to sue applies to state and local governments and state pension plans, but not to private pension plans or mutual funds holding shares for ordinary workers, so retirement savers in private plans do not get the exemption their public-sector counterparts received.

The counting rule treats a corporation, pension plan, partnership, or other entity as a single class member, so suits brought through institutions that pool many small investors are treated as if they represent one person.

Supporters' best argument, that a single national standard was needed to stop forum shopping and abusive parallel suits after the 1995 reforms, is a real cost that an honest backer would cite; but the law's practical effect was to remove the last plaintiff-friendly venue for securities fraud claims, and Congress chose issuer protection over investor recovery.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a genuine argument on the companies' side: Congress found that suits had migrated to state courts specifically to escape the 1995 federal reforms, and a patchwork of 50 state rules can invite duplicative and extortionate litigation. But the law stacked a second layer of protection on issuers who had already won sweeping procedural advantages in 1995, and the people who lose the most are defrauded investors, including workers whose retirement funds hold the shares. The protections for state regulators and state pension plans are real but narrow. On balance, the costs to investors outweigh the uniformity benefits the bill's supporters cited.

outcome.mechanism: It passed both chambers by wide margins, survived a conference committee, and the President signed it into law on November 3, 1998.

narrative.text: The Senate passed the bill 79-21 on May 13, 1998, with 53 of 55 Republicans and 26 of 45 Democrats voting yes.
The House took up the Senate bill on July 22, 1998, struck its contents and inserted the text of a similar House bill, and passed it without objection.

A conference committee reconciled the versions; the Senate agreed to the conference report by unanimous consent, and the House agreed 319-82 on October 13, 1998, with 213 of 227 Republicans and 106 of 206 Democrats in favor.
President Clinton signed the bill on November 3, 1998, and it became Public Law 105-353.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Publicly traded companies, their executives and directors, and their liability insurers came out ahead: they gained protection from state-court securities fraud class actions. The securities plaintiffs' bar came out on the losing side.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Public companies, their executives, and insurers

against.what_they_did: Pressed to preserve state enforcement authority; the final bill kept their investigative and enforcement powers intact.

sides.party_line_note: Republicans were nearly unanimous, 53-2 in the Senate and 213-1 in the House, while Democrats split, 26-19 yes in the Senate and 106-80 yes in the House, giving the bill large bipartisan majorities despite most opponents being Democrats.

industries.industry: Publicly traded corporations (and their directors-and-officers liability insurers)
industries.note: The law shields them from state-law securities fraud class actions and channels any covered case into federal court, where the 1995 rules already made suits much harder, cutting their settlement and defense exposure. The cost falls on shareholders and retirement savers who were defrauded.

State courts had become their main venue after the 1995 federal reforms; this law eliminates that docket for nationally traded stocks. Their income depends on recoveries for defrauded investors, so their loss tracks the loss to investors, even though fee incentives in this field drew legitimate criticism.

industries.industry: Public pension funds and state and local governments
industries.note: The bill carves them out: they can still sue on their own behalf or as a class of government entities, a right denied to private pension funds and mutual funds holding workers' savings. Public-employee retirement money thus kept a remedy that private-sector retirement money lost.

The bill reauthorizes SEC appropriations of $351,280,000 for fiscal 1999 and lets the agency hire and pay professional economists outside standard civil-service rules, while repealing statutory EDGAR filing requirements and leaving the system to the agency's own design.
